newsitem.title: UK: Investors on hold as flood concerns grip Poland.
newsitem.headline: Investors on hold as flood concerns grip Poland.

text.p: Heavy flooding has added to Poland's already uncertain investment climate following recent concern about a ballooning current account deficit and looming national elections.

Strategists and fund managers said on Friday that Poland, caught up in broader worries about current account deficits in emerging markets, was unlikely to attract fresh foreign investor support in the short term.

"I think there are going to be a lot of investors who hold on because they believe the long-term story, but bringing new money in right now is going to be hard, and you have the forecast of possible additional floods in the next week or two," said Roger Monson, chief equity strategist at Daiwa Europe.
The Polish zloty lost more then four percent on Tuesday before picking up slightly later in the week.
Two weeks of heavy flooding have raised concern about the prospect of increasing the budget deficit to cover the cost of relief.
Foreign & Colonial Emerging Markets said the flooding, worries about the budget and current account deficits and contagious currency panic from the Far East had resulted in volatility.
"There could be some additional pressure (on the zloty), especially if we get some nasty surprises on the budget deficit because of the flood expenses," said Monson.

"But it would have to be really bad -- such as over six percent of GDP -- before people would start really acting on that because most people will recognise that a chunk of this will be one-off type expense, and therefore not something to judge the government's performance on for the longer term."

David Mars, director of emerging Europe and Africa economics research at SBC Warburg, said the Polish central bank was likely to be relatively happy with the easier exchange rate because it allowed the bank to raise official rates if politicians were undisciplined on spending before the general election in September.
"I would be a bit nervous if I was running the central bank but I wouldn't be unhappy," Mars said.
Poland's money and foreign exchange markets are braced for a possible interest rate rise in the near future.
Most analysts in Poland see official interest rates rising one or two percentage points to curb credit growth and offset the effects of extra spending on flood relief.
Mars said the flooding would normally have had only a modest impact on sentiment, but other worries had increased its significance.

"It is the straw that breaks the camel's back. It could break the Czech back and that might almost be justifiable because these guys haven't done anything to remedy the situation. Of course it could break the Poles but that would not be justifiable.
"But there is no reason to expect fairness in this world and I think the Poles are aware of that," said Mars.

He said a sharp drop in the zloty would offer a buying opportunity, particularly if it coincided with an increase in interest rates, while any pick-ups in the Czech crown may still present opportunities.

Monson said the current account deficit was not at a stage where another Czech crisis would occur. "But if the deficit grows instead of flattens out or begins to shrink a bit, then within 12 months we might have to think seriously about a Czech example."
He said Poland would have to manage a slightly more aggressive decline in the zloty so that it could enhance export competitiveness.

Monson said his strategy on Poland was slightly better than neutral, based on what was still expected to be good economic growth over the longer term, some good company results, further improvements in inflation, and a credible central bank.
The equity market was also slightly cheaper than the Czech market and quite a bit cheaper than Hungary.
Monson said unhelpful inflation figures recently and elections in September had added to pressure on the currency.
